verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse.sanskrit: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥
verse.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verse.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.
verse.why: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

prasang.title: The glory of knowledge
prasang.summary: Krishna praises knowledge: learn it humbly from those who know, it carries even the worst wrongdoer across, faith and self-control bring it, and doubt destroys. He ends: cut your doubt and stand up.
prasang.lesson: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna is caught in grief and confusion about his duty. Krishna tells him to learn from those who have seen the truth. He says to approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve. This is how knowledge is passed on and doubt is cut through. The point is that understanding does not come from pride or force. It comes from bowing down, from real inquiry, and from doing the work of service.
verse.for_you: This is a good place to start, because you are willing to learn rather than argue. The texts offer a way through confusion when you approach them with humility and a real question.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you feel certain about an answer, and ask what you might still not know.
verse.scene_line: You are on the battlefield of your own questions, ready to learn from those who have seen the truth.
asks: How do I approach these texts with humility?
How do I separate my own opinions from the text's voice?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: यतः प्रवृत्तिर्भूतानां येन सर्वमिदं ततम् । स्वकर्मणा तमभ्यर्च्य सिद्धिं विन्दति मानवः ॥
verse.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
verse.translation: By worshipping, through his own work, Him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Work as worship doesn't mean overwork or tolerating exploitation.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna that every person has a path suited to their nature. He says that a person reaches perfection when they worship the source of all life through the work they are already doing. The point is to offer your own work, with all its flaws, as a form of devotion. The story notes that every path has its own difficulties, and one's own path, however imperfect, is better than trying to walk in another's shoes.
verse.for_you: You are trying to understand these texts so you can explain your view to your cousin. This verse suggests that your own path of learning and working is its own form of worship. You do not need to perform a grand ritual.
verse.try_today: Notice one small task at work and offer it as your own form of worship.
verse.scene_line: You are at your desk, offering your own work as your worship.
asks: What does it mean to offer my own work as worship?
How do I keep my own path when others expect me to follow theirs?
Can my own work be its own form of worship?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.line: Unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger: that is a steady mind.
verse.translation: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who has no craving for pleasures, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.
verse.misuse: A steady mind still feels; it just isn't run by sorrow, fear or anger.

matched.label: I'm anxious about how things will turn out

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Arjuna wants to know what a steady mind looks like. Krishna tells him it is not a mind without feeling, but one that is not ruled by sorrow or pleasure. It is free of clinging, fear and anger. This steadiness is not a gift you wait for. It is built by guarding what you pay attention to. When you dwell on a loss or a slight, anger grows. When you guard your attention, you guard your mind.
verse.for_you: You are trying to hold a steady view about your cousin and marriage while the family pressure is loud. The text says steadiness is not about ignoring the noise. It is about not letting the noise run your mind.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind starts clinging to what your cousin said. Let the thought pass without feeding it.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting with a question that will not let you go, and the mind wants to cling.
asks: How do I stop the mind from clinging to a family argument?
What does it mean to guard my attention in a conversation?
Can I be steady and still care about the outcome?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.sanskrit: देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा । तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
verse.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, just after Arjuna has laid down his bow in grief and confusion. Krishna tells Arjuna that the soul inside the body is not born, and it does not die. It simply moves from one body to another, just as a person moves from childhood to youth to old age. The one who truly understands this does not lose their balance when loss comes.
verse.for_you: You are trying to hold a view that birth does not divide the self, while your cousin sees caste as a fixed wall. The Gita says the self is one continuous thread, wearing different bodies like different clothes.
verse.scene_line: You stand at a crossroads where a cousin's marriage meets the truth of an undivided self.
asks: How do I explain this to my cousin without fighting?
What does it mean to see the self in someone I disagree with?
Does this mean my own caste identity is not real?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: सर्वभूतस्थमात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि । ईक्षते योगयुक्तात्मा सर्वत्र समदर्शनः ॥
verse.line: See yourself in every being and every being in yourself, and you see the same everywhere.
verse.translation: One whose self is joined in yoga sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self; he sees the same everywhere.
verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to settle the mind into yoga. He says that a person who has united their self in yoga sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and therefore sees the same everywhere. The point is that this vision comes through moderation and gentle return, again and again, settling the mind.
verse.for_you: You are trying to read the text for your cousin, but the text wants you to read it for yourself. It asks you to see the same self in the girl your cousin wants, and in the cousin who wants her. That is the only purity the text speaks of.
verse.try_today: Notice one person at work and see them as a self, not a role.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting with your cousin, and the question is whether you can see the self in both of you.
asks: How do I see the same self in someone my family rejects?
Can I see the self in my cousin without losing my own view?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.meaning: Krishna is explaining the three kinds of austerity to Arjuna, and here he names the discipline of speech. The verse says that speech which causes no distress, which is true, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts, is called austerity of speech. This means your words should heal rather than harm, carry truth without cruelty, and build up rather than tear down. It asks you to examine not just what you say, but the intention behind it, so that your speech becomes a steady practice rather than a weapon or a performance.
verse.for_you: You are trying to explain your view on caste to your cousin, and the words you choose now matter. You want to be understood without starting a fight, and to speak the truth of what the Gita teaches about the self. Let your speech be a bridge, not a wall.
verse.try_today: Before you speak to your cousin, check if your words are true, kind and helpful.
verse.scene_line: You are at the table with your cousin, choosing the words that will either build a bridge or a wall.
asks: How do I say the truth without wounding my cousin?
What if my cousin only wants to hear their own view?

story.title: Arjuna asks to see the cosmic form
story.story_hook: His confusion gone, Arjuna made a bold request of his friend: show me who you really are.
story.summary: Thanking Krishna for dispelling his confusion, Arjuna asks to see his imperishable form if he is able.
story.lesson: Ask humbly for what you long to see.
